detail: supported
This method treats a neural depth renderer $f$ as a conditional Directed Distance Field (DDF) by mapping camera parameters $\Pi$ and scene shapes $\Lambda_S$ to depth and visibility images [S1].

The claim accurately reflects the content of Source [S1]. The source explicitly defines the neural depth renderer $f$ as a function mapping camera parameters ($Π$) and shapes ($Λ_S$) to depth and visibility images, and states that 'f is implicitly a conditional DDF'. It further explains that pixel values are computed as $(d(p, v), ξ(p, v))$ where $p$ and $v$ are determined by the camera parameters.
supported
Builds on DDF properties to apply them to neural rendering frameworks [S1].

The claim states that the work builds on DDF properties to apply them to neural rendering frameworks. The evidence explicitly states that a neural depth renderer is treated as a conditional DDF and that 'all the properties of DDFs hold in these cases as well.' It further mentions that this view allows DDF properties (like Property II and III) to apply to differentiable neural rendering frameworks and that this perspective can improve the framework for differentiable neural rendering. Thus, every fact in the claim is supported by the evidence.
supported
- Camera Parameters $\Pi$: Defines the ray origin $p$ (center of projection) and ray direction $v$ (pixel direction from $p$ into the scene) [S1].

The claim states that Camera Parameters Π define the ray origin p (center of projection) and ray direction v (pixel direction from p into the scene). The evidence in Source [S1] explicitly confirms this by stating: 'p and v are a fixed function of Π... with p determined by the centre of projection (camera position) and v determined by the direction corresponding to that pixel, from the centre of projection out into the scene.' Thus, every fact in the claim is present in the evidence.
supported
- The formulation holds regardless of the internal architecture of $f$ [S1].

The claim states that the formulation holds regardless of the internal architecture of $f$. The evidence in Source [S1] explicitly states: 'In other words, the camera intrinsics and extrinsics determine the p and v value for each pixel, with p determined by the centre of projection (camera position) and v determined by the direction corresponding to that pixel, from the centre of projection out into the scene. We may thus regard the depth pixel value as a function of p and v, via the camera parameters. This holds regardless of the architecture of f.' This directly supports the claim.
supported
- Ray Origin: $p = \text{CenterOfProjection}(\Pi)$ [S1].

The claim states that the origin of the ray $p$ is the CenterOfProjection($Π$). The evidence in Source [S1] explicitly states: '...with p determined by the centre of projection (camera position)...'. This directly supports the claim that $p$ corresponds to the center of projection defined by the camera parameters $Π$.
supported
Evaluate the neural renderer $f(\Pi, \Lambda_S)$ to obtain the depth $d$ and visibility $\xi$ for the ray $(p, v)$ [S1].

The claim states that the neural renderer $f$ is evaluated to obtain depth $d$ and visibility $ eta$ (represented as $d$ and $xi$ in the evidence) for a ray defined by $(p, v)$. Source [S1] explicitly defines the function $f$ as mapping to an image where each pixel value is computed as $(d(p, v), xi(p, v))$, with $p$ and $v$ determined by camera parameters. The evidence confirms that the output of the renderer for a specific ray direction and center of projection consists of depth and visibility values.
supported
Proposed to parallelize DDFs and improve the framework for differentiable neural rendering of geometric quantities [S1].

The claim states that the source proposes to parallelize DDFs and improve the framework for differentiable neural rendering of geometric quantities. The evidence in Source [S1] explicitly asks 'how to parallelize a DDF' and concludes with the statement: 'We believe this point of view can improve the framework for differentiable neural rendering of geometric quantities'. Both parts of the claim are directly present in the text.
supported
- Pixel Value: $(d(p, v), \xi(p, v))$ [S1].

The claim states that the pixel value is $(d(p, v), ξ(p, v))$ and cites Source [S1]. The evidence in Source [S1] explicitly states: 'each pixel value can be computed as (d(p, v), ξ(p, v)), where p and v are a fixed function of Π ∈ ΛΠ.' It further clarifies that 'p determined by the centre of projection (camera position) and v determined by the direction corresponding to that pixel'. This matches the claim's description of p as the camera center of projection and v as the ray direction determined by camera intrinsics/extrinsics.
supported
Assign the pixel value $(d(p, v), \xi(p, v))$ [S1].

The claim states that the pixel value is assigned as $(d(p, v), ξ(p, v))$. The evidence in Source [S1] explicitly states: 'each pixel value can be computed as (d(p, v), ξ(p, v))'. It further clarifies that $p$ is the camera center of projection and $v$ is the ray direction. This matches the claim exactly.
supported

It differs from standard neural rendering by explicitly framing output pixels as functions of ray origins and directions derived from camera parameters, thereby inheriting DDF properties such as the relationship between depth gradients and surface normals [S1].

The claim states that the method differs from standard neural rendering by framing output pixels as functions of ray origins and directions derived from camera parameters, inheriting DDF properties like the relationship between depth gradients and surface normals. Source [S1] explicitly confirms this: it states that 'each pixel value can be computed as (d(p, v), ξ(p, v)), where p and v are a fixed function of Π' (camera parameters), with p being the center of projection (origin) and v being the ray direction. It further states that 'all the properties of DDFs hold in these cases as well: for example... Property II relates ∂Cp Id to the surface normals image.' Thus, every factual component of the claim is present in the evidence.
supported
- Output: An $m$-pixel image where each pixel contains a tuple $(d(p, v), \xi(p, v))$, with $d \in \mathbb{R}^+$ (depth) and $\xi \in [0, 1]$ (visibility) [S1].

The claim states that the output is an $m$-pixel image where each pixel contains a tuple $(d(p, v), ξ(p, v))$, with $d ∈ ℝ^+$ (depth) and $ξ ∈ [0, 1]$ (visibility). Source [S1] explicitly defines the function $f$ mapping to an image space $I_{d,ξ} = ℝ^+ × [0, 1]$ (an $m$-pixel image) and states that 'each pixel value can be computed as $(d(p, v), ξ(p, v))$'. The definitions of $d$ as depth (implied by $ℝ^+$ and context of depth images) and $ξ$ as visibility (implied by $[0, 1]$ and context) match the claim exactly.
supported
- Ray Direction: $v = \text{RayDirection}(p, \text{PixelIndex}, \text{Intrinsics}(\Pi))$ [S1].

The evidence explicitly states that 'v is determined by the direction corresponding to that pixel, from the centre of projection out into the scene' and that 'p and v are a fixed function of Π'. This directly supports the claim that the ray direction $v$ is a function of the pixel index (implied by 'corresponding to that pixel') and the intrinsics/extrinsics (represented by Π).
supported
- For mesh data extraction, $(\xi, d)$ is obtained via ray-triangle intersection after computing $(p, v)$ [S1].

The claim states that for mesh data extraction, $(p, v)$ is computed first, and then $(ξ, d)$ is obtained via ray-triangle intersection. The provided text from Source [S1], specifically under the section 'A. Mesh Data Extraction', explicitly states: 'note that we only need to obtain (p, v), after which (ξ, d) can be obtained via raytriangle intersection'. This directly supports the claim.
supported
- Shape $\Lambda_S$: The geometric representation queried by the renderer [S1].

The claim states that the geometric representation queried by the renderer is denoted as Shape $Λ_S$. The evidence in Source [S1] explicitly defines the function $f$ as mapping from continuous camera parameters ($Λ_Π$) and 'some space of shapes $Λ_S$' to images. It further clarifies that $f$ is a neural depth renderer treating these inputs. Thus, the evidence confirms that $Λ_S$ represents the space of shapes (geometric representation) used as input to the renderer.
supported
For each pixel, compute the ray origin $p$ and direction $v$ as fixed functions of $\Pi$ [S1].

The claim states that for each pixel, the ray origin $p$ and direction $v$ are computed as fixed functions of the camera parameters $Π$. The evidence in Source [S1] explicitly states: 'each pixel value can be computed as (d(p, v), ξ(p, v)), where p and v are a fixed function of Π ∈ ΛΠ.' It further clarifies that 'the camera intrinsics and extrinsics determine the p and v value for each pixel.' This directly supports the claim.
